description: We're Wizor Space, a team of curious people building predictive tech for extreme environments in space. Last year we were national standouts and Global Nominees at NASA Space Apps. This year: health, safety & well-being monitoring for astronauts, combining biometric and environmental data to anticipate fatigue, stress and human error. Into space, AI or real impact? Join us! We’re looking for game dev, data science, UX/UI and hardware skills. We value curiosity, good vibes and teamwork.
summary: Astronauts report operational facts, but rarely say "I'm exhausted" or "I'm scared". Smart Wilson is an intelligent AI health companion that closes that gap. It listens to how the astronaut speaks, feels and decides, not only to what they say, and compares their voice with their own training baseline. It fuses that with vital signs, habitat conditions and NASA space-weather data to tell effort from fear, assign one of four levels (green, yellow, orange, red) and recommend one clear action: prevention, next step or survival. When Earth is reachable, Mission Control has the final word. When it is not, Smart Wilson guides the crew with pre-approved actions, the astronaut can always override it, and every decision is logged, but Smart Wilson accompanies the crew every step of the way. This is not a rare case: at the lunar south pole, where Artemis crews will land, Earth is below the horizon about two weeks every month. Our web prototype lets anyone run nine lunar-surface scenarios with astronaut Amy and then see, from Mission Control, why Wilson acted. The same approach can protect workers in mining, oil and gas and remote analog missions.
details:
What it does. Smart Wilson is an AI health companion for astronauts on the lunar surface. Astronauts are trained to stay calm and to report in operational terms, so fatigue, pain or fear often go unsaid. Wilson reads three channels from the astronaut, in order of reliability: short codes (for example, E-MED for a medical emergency or P2 for physical discomfort), spoken words, and voice analysis (pitch, intensity, rhythm and pauses compared with the astronaut's own training baseline). It fuses them with vital signs, habitat and suit conditions, and NASA space-weather data.

How it works. A fast path reacts in seconds to emergency codes, words such as "my chest hurts" or critical vital signs. A weighted neural network (moment of the task, physiological condition, environmental condition and biometric data) assigns one of four levels (green, yellow, orange, red), an action type (prevention, next step or survival), an escalation path and Wilson's spoken response, each backed by prior training and behavior experience, and NASA standards (such as NASA-STD-3001). With a link to Earth, Mission Control has the final word. Without it, Wilson guides the crew with pre-approved actions, the astronaut can always override it, and everything is logged for review. This is routine at the lunar south pole: without relay satellites, Earth is below the horizon about two weeks every month. Because those gaps are predictable, Wilson can also recommend scheduling the riskiest tasks inside communication windows.

What you can try. Our web prototype runs a sample with nine scenarios (three moments of an EVA and three states of astronaut Amy: physical stress, psychological stress and life risk). Each run shows Wilson's response and then, in the Mission Control view, which data led to the decision and who made it. A separate voice monitor shows the voice analysis. The digital twin, live suit telemetry, the astronaut codes and the wearable hardware (chest unit and forearm display) are part of the product design and are documented.

Benefits and impact. It addresses a gap NASA itself describes: behavioral health needs continuous, minimally invasive monitoring, while current support relies on periodic private conferences. Telling effort from fear changes the right action, and an early, explained recommendation can prevent an emergency. On Earth, the same engine with a different environment profile can protect workers in remote and extreme settings such as mining, oil and gas and polar or analog missions, where connectivity is also intermittent.

Creativity and what we considered. Wilson is a companion, not a dashboard: it speaks first with the action and then with support, tells the astronaut whether an instruction comes from Mission Control or from Wilson, and never lets a self-reported "I'm fine" hide a critical reading. We considered privacy (private conversations reach Mission Control only as a level), accessibility (color is always paired with text, sound and blink pattern), and limits: thresholds still need validation with astronauts and flight surgeons.

Tools. HTML and JavaScript web prototypes, Web Speech API, Vercel, GitHub, Google Workspace and Claude (Anthropic) for research, documentation and code, Eleven labs for voices generation.
